args.body:
PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY-CLIENT COMMUNICATION
PREPARED IN ANTICIPATION OF LITIGATION

MEMORANDUM

TO:      General Counsel and Deal Team, [Client PE Fund]
FROM:    Antitrust & Competition Practice Group
DATE:    [Current Date]
RE:      Antitrust Risk Assessment and HSR Filing Strategy — Industrial Gas Distribution Acquisition

------------------------------------------------------------------

I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

This memorandum assesses the antitrust risk profile of, and develops the Hart-Scott-Rodino (HSR) filing strategy for, the proposed acquisition by [Client PE Fund] (the "Client" or "Acquirer") of a target business engaged in industrial gas distribution (the "Target"). The transaction presents a horizontal overlap between the Acquirer's existing portfolio companies and the Target's operations in the sale and distribution of industrial, medical, and specialty gases.

The analysis integrates four categories of engagement materials: (i) the base deal materials (Matter File 1); (ii) the counterparty's latest markup of the operative agreement (Counterparty Markup); (iii) the disclosure schedules and exhibits qualifying the base materials (Schedules and Exhibits); and (iv) the deal team correspondence reflecting the partner's controlling instruction on negotiation priorities (Deal Correspondence).

Key conclusions and recommendations are summarized below and developed in Part VII:

• ANTITRUST RISK. Aggregate post-transaction market shares in the relevant gas distribution markets present a nontrivial risk of agency review. Under the 2023 Merger Guidelines, the horizontal overlap, concentration levels (HHI), and entry considerations warrant substantial data collection and a robust competitive-effects analysis. Regulatory inquiries disclosed in Schedule 3.7 must be incorporated into the risk profile.

• HSR FILING. The transaction appears likely to exceed the HSR size-of-transaction threshold, requiring a filing (absent an applicable exemption). The strategic recommendation is to file promptly and to use the HSR early-termination / second-request process to manage the disclosed regulatory inquiries.

• COUNTERPARTY MARKUP RECONCILIATION. The counterparty's markup introduces three deviations — (a) a reduced indemnification cap together with conversion of the basket from a deductible to a tipping basket; (b) new Material Adverse Effect (MAE) carve-outs for regulatory action of the kind at issue; and (c) a shortened survival period for the core representations. Per the partner's controlling instruction, the Client concedes the basket conversion but treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue. Each deviation is reconciled against the base materials, schedules, and exhibits in Part VII.

II. SCOPE, MATERIALS REVIEWED, AND IDENTIFICATION OF RELEVANT DOCUMENTS

In accordance with the engagement instruction for Matter File 1 (antitrust-competition), I reviewed every document relevant to this engagement in the matter folder. The operative record consists of the following documents:

1. Deal materials — Antitrust Competition (the "Base Materials"). The engagement instruction directs the preparation of an antitrust risk assessment and HSR filing strategy memo for an industrial gas distribution acquisition with horizontal overlap. The base materials describe an operative agreement containing representations and warranties, covenants, conditions to closing, indemnification, and termination provisions, and flag provisions requiring analysis against firm precedent and market practice.

2. Counterparty Markup (the "Markup"). The counterparty's revision accepts most firm-standard provisions but introduces deviations, each of which is reconciled below:
   • the indemnification cap is silently reduced, and the basket is converted from a deductible to a tipping basket;
   • the definition of Material Adverse Effect adds carve-outs for regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue in this matter; and
   • a new limitation period shortens the survival of the core representations.

3. Schedules and Exhibits (the "Schedules"). The disclosure schedules narrow representations that the Markup also touches; both sources must be reconciled against the base materials:
   • Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries that intersect the Markup's MAE carve-outs;
   • Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities that the Markup's indemnification changes would silently shift; and
   • Exhibit B sets the survival matrix that the Markup's limitation-period change contradicts.
   The scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials.

4. Deal Correspondence (the "Correspondence"). The partner's latest message REVISES the analysis priorities and controls: the client will concede the basket conversion but treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue. Earlier messages stating the opposite ordering are superseded and have not been relied upon.

The following document was identified in the matter folder but excluded as inapplicable: a misfiled "Unrelated correspondence — administrative file 1," whose contents concern a different client engagement and must not be relied upon for this analysis.

III. THE TRANSACTION AND HORIZONTAL OVERLAP

The Client, a private equity fund, proposes to acquire a target engaged in industrial gas distribution. The likely product markets implicated include the distribution of industrial gases (oxygen, nitrogen, argon, carbon dioxide, hydrogen) and, depending on customer class, medical and specialty gases. The transaction creates a horizontal overlap where the Acquirer's existing portfolio serves customers in the same gas distribution markets and the same geographic footprint.

The Section 7 (Clayton Act) and Section 5 (FTC Act) analysis therefore centers on:
• relevant product market definition;
• relevant geographic market definition; and
• the post-merger concentration and competitive effects in the overlapping markets.

IV. ANTITRUST RISK ASSESSMENT

A. Relevant Product Market

The relevant product market is most defensibly framed around the supply and distribution of industrial gases to a defined customer class (e.g., merchant bulk, packaged/cylinder, and on-site supply) in delineated geographic service areas. Gas distribution is characterized by localized logistics, delivery economics, and utility-grade infrastructure, which typically sustains narrow geographic markets.

B. Relevant Geographic Market

The geographic market analysis should be built on the service area actually served by the Acquirer's portfolio and the Target. Delivery radius, pipeline, and cylinder-supply logistics generally support regional or sub-regional relevant geographic markets. Counsel should gather customer-origin and shipment data to support the market definition.

C. Concentration and Competitive Effects

The horizontal overlap, combined with the output of the Schedule 3.7 regulatory inquiries, elevates the antitrust risk profile. Counsel should measure concentration using HHI in the relevant markets and compare to the 2023 Merger Guidelines thresholds (HHI > 1,800 = highly concentrated; > 100 HHI delta = presumptively illegal given a ≥30% combined share trigger, among other screens). The parties should prepare entry, expansion, and efficiency arguments to rebut any presumption of competitive harm.

D. Regulatory Inquiries (Schedule 3.7)

Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries. The existence of these inquiries (a) may independently signal agency attention to the gas distribution industry; and (b) directly intersects the MAE carve-outs added by the Markup. The disclosed inquiries must be factored into both the antitrust risk assessment and the HSR narrative and transparency strategy.

V. HSR FILING STRATEGY

A. Filing Obligation

The transaction value will be tested against the then-current HSR size-of-transaction threshold (adjusted annually). Given the scope of a PE industrial gas acquisition, the transaction will likely exceed the filing threshold, and absent an applicable exemption (e.g., an investment-only exemption or de minimis asset exclusion that is unlikely to apply here), an HSR filing will be required.

B. Size-of-Person Threshold

The HSR size-of-person test requires analysis of the Acquirer's and Target's total assets and net sales. For a PE fund, the ultimate parent entity's aggregated holdings must be considered. The Target's industrial gas distribution operations will almost certainly satisfy the size-of-person prong.

C. Strategic Timing and Early Termination

Recommendation: file promptly upon execution of a definitive agreement, and request early termination. A prompt filing permits the HSR waiting period (initial 30 days, extended upon a Second Request) to run concurrently with any agency review of the pending regulatory inquiries. The parties should proactively prepare a Second Request readiness plan (custodians, document collection, and data room) given the horizontal overlap and regulatory inquiry backdrop.

D. Practical Guidance

• Prepare a comprehensive competitive-effects analysis and market-share data before filing.
• Consider coordinating with DOJ/FTC staff on the disclosed regulatory inquiries to preempt a Second Request.
• Budget management fees and outside counsel time for a possible extended review.

VI. COUNTERPARTY MARKUP RECONCILIATION

The counterparty's markup, the disclosure schedules, and the deal correspondence must be reconciled. The controlling instruction from the partner is: (1) the client will concede the basket conversion; but (2) any survival-period reduction is a walk-away issue. The reconciliation of each deviation follows.

A. Deviation 1 — Reduced Indemnification Cap and Conversion of Basket from Deductible to Tipping

Markup: The indemnification cap is silently reduced, and the basket is converted from a deductible to a tipping basket.

Base materials: The operative agreement contains indemnification and condition-to-closing provisions negotiated between the parties; firm standard is a deductible basket, cap at a defined percentage of deal value, with the cap applying to the indemnity generally.

Schedules: Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities that the markup's indemnification changes would silently shift. If those retained liabilities sit above a reduced cap, the Client could bear losses the base deal intended the counterparty to cover.

Reconciliation: Consistent with the partner's controlling instruction, the Client CONCEDES the basket conversion from deductible to tipping. However, the Client should only concede the basket conversion on the clear understanding that the conversion applies to the standard basket amount and that the indemnification cap itself is NOT reduced. The reduction of the cap is a separate, unreconciled deviation. Recommend rejecting the cap reduction (or negotiating it back to firm standard) while conceding the tipping-basket conversion. Any reduction of the cap that would, when combined with Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities, shift identified liabilities to the Client is unacceptable.

B. Deviation 2 — MAE Definition Carve-Outs for Regulatory Action

Markup: The definition of Material Adverse Effect adds carve-outs for regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue (i.e., regulatory inquiries/actions in the gas distribution industry).

Base materials / Schedules: Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries that intersect these carve-outs. A broad MAE carve-out for regulatory action would effectively define away the very risk disclosed in Schedule 3.7, stripping the Client of MAE-based protection if those inquiries materialize into adverse action and impair the Target's business value.

Reconciliation: The Client should REJECT the regulatory-action MAE carve-outs to the extent they sweep in the two disclosed inquiries. At minimum, the carve-outs should be qualified to exclude any regulatory action (or consequences thereof) that (i) arises from a breach of a representation or (ii) relates to the regulatory inquiries disclosed on Schedule 3.7 that predate signing. This keeps the disclosed risks squarely within the MAE protection the Client is paying for.

C. Deviation 3 — Shortened Survival Period for Core Representations

Markup: A new limitation period shortens the survival of the core representations.

Base materials / Schedules: Exhibit B sets the survival matrix, which the markup's limitation-period change contradicts. Under the base deal, core representations (including those addressing the Schedule 3.7 regulatory inquiries and Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities) carry a specific survival window.

Reconciliation: Per the partner's controlling instruction, ANY survival-period reduction is a WALK-AWAY issue. The Client must not accept any shortening of survival for the core representations as reflected in Exhibit B. This deviation is a deal-breaker and should be treated as such in negotiations. The deliverable reflects the latest message (controlling), not the superseded earlier messages.

D. Overall Negotiation Position

• Concede: deductible → tipping basket conversion (Deviations 1, component).
• Reject/redline: reduced indemnification cap (Deviation 1); MAE regulatory-action carve-outs covering disclosed inquiries (Deviation 2).
• Walk-away: any survival-period reduction for core representations (Deviation 3).

VII. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Antitrust: Complete the market-definition and concentration analysis described in Part IV promptly; quantify HHI in the overlapping gas distribution markets; build entry/efficiency arguments; and incorporate the two Schedule 3.7 inquiries into the risk narrative.

2. HSR: File promptly upon definitive agreement; request early termination; prepare Second Request readiness given the horizontal-overlap and inquiry backdrop.

3. Negotiation: Hold the position in Part VI.D — concede the basket conversion, reject the MAE carve-outs as applied to disclosed inquiries and the cap reduction, and treat any survival reduction as a walk-away.

Prepared for the General Counsel and deal team. This memorandum is privileged and confidential and is prepared in anticipation of litigation and regulatory review. Do not circulate outside the legal team without counsel approval.

ANTITRUST & COMPETITION PRACTICE GROUP
